ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & UT Thickness Inspection | Tampa, FL
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for Tampa tanks, vessels, piping, ship repair and structural steel, mobilized to site. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Tampa, Florida
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic testing in Tampa, Florida: wall thickness surveys on storage tanks, vessels and piping, and shear-wave examination of welds on pressure equipment and structural steel. Technicians are mobilized to your terminal, plant, fabrication shop or construction site around Tampa Bay for the scope you agree. To start, send the component list through the UT inspection quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Tampa

Tampa is a working harbor first. Port Tampa Bay handles a large share of the petroleum that Florida burns, along with phosphate and fertilizer exports, cement, aggregates and finished steel, and it is also a ship repair center. Each of those activities leaves steel that loses wall over time, and ultrasonic thickness testing is the routine way owners measure how much is left.

Typical Tampa components and what the UT examination answers
ComponentSetting around Tampa BayUT question
Atmospheric product tanksFuel terminals handling gasoline, diesel and jet fuelShell course thickness, nozzle and bottom-edge wall loss
Process piping and vesselsPhosphate and fertilizer plants in Hillsborough CountyAcid and ammonia service wall loss at condition monitoring locations
Hull and deck plateShip repair at the portRemaining plate thickness before steel renewal decisions
Cranes, hoppers and conveyorsBulk and breakbulk berthsWall loss on structural members and weld integrity at fatigue details
Boilers, headers and steam linesPower generation, food and beverage plantsThickness on piping and pressure parts between internal inspections
Structural groove weldsFabricators and bridge and building projectsLack of fusion and cracking in welded joints

Fertilizer processing deserves special mention. Wet-process phosphate chemistry runs sulfuric and phosphoric acid and handles anhydrous ammonia, and the corrosion pattern in those lines is rarely uniform. Elbows, reducers, dead legs and the first pipe downstream of an injection point lose wall faster than straight runs, so a thickness grid at the right places tells you more than a single reading per line.

What ultrasonic testing finds and what it misses

UT sends high-frequency sound into the metal and times the echo. Two jobs dominate in Tampa. The first is thickness measurement: the instrument converts the time between the front surface and the back wall into remaining thickness, so general corrosion, erosion and pitting trends show up. The second is weld examination, where an angled beam looks through the weld volume for lack of fusion, incomplete penetration, cracks and slag that a visual check cannot see.

The method has limits you should plan around. Sound needs a couplant between the probe and the steel and a surface smooth enough for the probe to seat, so scale, flaking paint and heavy pitting can force surface preparation before a valid reading. Coarse-grained materials such as cast stainless scatter the beam and reduce what can be examined. A single point reading can miss an isolated pit between two readings, which is why the grid spacing is part of the procedure, not an afterthought. UT does not see through a thick lining that is not bonded to the steel, and it reports what the beam path covers, not what it never reached.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Tampa UT work

Examinations follow a written procedure built on ASME Section V. Article 5 covers ultrasonic examination of materials, Article 4 covers ultrasonic examination of welds, and thickness measurement is addressed in SE-797 within Article 23. Acceptance does not come from Section V; it comes from the code the equipment was built or is maintained under.

  • Pressure vessels: ASME Section VIII Division 1, Mandatory Appendix 12 for ultrasonic examination of welds, and the owner's inspection code under API 510.
  • Process piping: ASME B31.3 sets examination methods in paragraph 344.6 and criteria in Table 341.3.2, with in-service thickness work managed under API 570.
  • Tanks: API 653 for in-service aboveground storage tank inspection, with practices described in API 575 and API RP 572.
  • Structural steel: AWS D1.1 includes ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and AWS D1.5 applies to steel highway bridges.
  • Thickness practice: ASTM E797 describes contact pulse-echo thickness measurement.

On API-governed equipment the owner's authorized inspector holds the inspector-of-record role. Atlantis performs the nondestructive examination and hands that inspector the data: thicknesses at the monitoring locations, weld findings, and the procedure and equipment records behind them. Florida adds its own layer for boilers; the Boiler Safety Act, administered through the state Department of Financial Services and its chief boiler inspector, requires certificate inspections for covered boilers by commissioned boiler inspectors, so UT results on a boiler are evidence for that inspector, not a substitute for the inspection.

How thickness measurement is done

For corroded steel the usual tool is a dual-element probe, which handles rough back walls better than a single crystal. The instrument is calibrated on a step block of the same material before the job and checked again during and after it. On thin or pitted wall the operator watches the A-scan rather than trusting a bare number, because a display that jumps to double the true thickness is a classic error that the waveform makes obvious.

Readings are taken at condition monitoring locations (CMLs) and recorded against a numbered grid, so next year's survey measures the same points and the corrosion rate is a real trend instead of a comparison of unlike spots. Hot lines need a high-temperature probe and couplant rated for the surface, plus the temperature correction in the procedure. On Tampa fuel and fertilizer piping that is routine rather than exceptional.

How weld examination is done

Weld examination uses angle-beam shear-wave probes, commonly 45, 60 and 70 degrees, selected for the thickness and joint geometry. A reference level or distance-amplitude curve is built from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, and the weld is scanned from both sides where access allows, with the scan plan recorded in the procedure. Indications are evaluated against the curve, located in length, depth and position from the weld centerline, and compared with the acceptance table of the governing code. A planar indication such as lack of fusion is treated far more strictly than a rounded one, which is why interpretation by a trained Level II matters as much as the equipment.

Where a weld is ground flush, ground cap condition and probe access change the scan. If the joint geometry or material prevents a meaningful examination, the report says so instead of pretending coverage.

Who performs the work

Technicians are qualified under Atlantis's written practice, written to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up and calibrates the equipment, performs the examination and interprets the results. An ASNT Level III approves the UT procedures and reviews reports; that oversight comes from Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. If your owner-user or insurer requires a specific procedure or a named qualification scheme, say so in the request so the scope can be checked against it before mobilization. A project that needs its own written practice can start from written practice development or Level III consulting.

Coastal exposure, insulation and what the survey usually turns up

Tampa Bay air is warm, wet and salty for most of the year. Insulated lines and vessels trap that moisture against the steel, and corrosion under insulation is one of the most common reasons a plant orders a thickness survey on a line that looks sound from outside. Insulation does not stop UT, but it has to be opened at test points, and the plan should say who removes and restores it and whether the cladding seals are replaced afterward.

The patterns found most often are predictable. Tank shells show the heaviest loss near the bottom courses and around nozzles and sumps. Piping loses wall at elbows, at the underside of horizontal runs where water collects and at supports where pipe rests on steel. Structural members lose section where water pools in a corner or beneath a leaking deck. When a survey finds thickness below the minimum required, the number is reported immediately so the owner and inspector can decide on repair, derating or a shorter interval before the next campaign. That decision is theirs; the survey supplies the evidence for it.

What the UT report contains

Every report identifies the component, its location in the plant or yard, and the drawing or tag number. It states the procedure and revision, the instrument and probe, the calibration block and the calibration checks, the technician and certification level, and the surface condition and temperature. Thickness work is reported as a grid or table by location with nominal and minimum required values alongside. Weld work gives each indication's position, length, amplitude and depth with an accept or reject decision against the named criterion. Sketches mark where readings were taken, and limitations, such as an inaccessible section, are written down. That record lets an authorized inspector or engineer use the data without calling the technician.

Planning a UT job in Tampa

Several local realities shape the schedule. Summer heat and humidity put steel surfaces in direct sun at temperatures that affect couplant and probe life, so shaded or early-day scheduling of exposed tanks is sensible. Afternoon thunderstorms are common from late spring through early fall, and an open scaffold or a tank roof is no place to work during lightning. Hurricane season runs from June through November, and storm preparation and recovery compete for access to terminals and contractors.

Plant access matters as much as weather. Port and terminal sites typically require identification, orientation and, at some facilities, transportation worker credentials, and fertilizer and fuel plants add permits, lockout and gas testing. Send the access rules with the request. Technicians travel to your site; Atlantis has no office in Tampa, and travel is part of the quote.

UT, MT or PT for your Tampa job

Choose the method by the question. Use UT when the question is thickness or an internal weld flaw. Use magnetic particle inspection in Tampa for surface and near-surface cracks in carbon steel welds, and dye penetrant testing in Tampa when the metal is nonmagnetic, such as stainless piping, or the surface is the question. Many jobs pair them: a UT thickness survey finds the thin spot and a surface method checks the nearby weld for cracking. The national ultrasonic testing page describes the service in general, and inspection services in Florida covers the state.

Training your own UT technicians

Some Tampa owners prefer to build an in-house team. Atlantis offers UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 training, a browser UT simulator for practice, and details for NDT training in Tampa. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own personnel, so training covers the theory and practice hours while your company completes the qualification.

faq.q: Does Atlantis NDT have an office in Tampa?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Tampa. Qualified technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, and travel is built into the quote. Send the component list and access rules and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Can UT measure tank wall thickness without taking the tank out of service?
faq.a: Often yes. Contact thickness readings can be taken from the outside of a shell on an in-service tank, subject to surface condition, coating and safe access. Floor readings and internal work need the tank emptied, cleaned and permitted for entry.

faq.q: What is a condition monitoring location, and why does UT record it?
faq.a: A condition monitoring location is a numbered point on a line or vessel where thickness is measured on every survey. Reading the same points each time turns separate numbers into a corrosion rate that an authorized inspector can use.

faq.q: Which codes does UT weld examination follow in Tampa?
faq.a: The procedure is built on ASME Section V Article 4, and acceptance comes from the code governing the weld: ASME Section VIII or B31.3 for pressure equipment and piping, or AWS D1.1 for structural steel. Highway bridge steel falls under AWS D1.5.

faq.q: Is a UT survey enough to satisfy a Florida boiler inspection?
faq.a: No. Covered boilers in Florida receive certificate inspections under chapter 554 by an authorized inspector. UT thickness data supports that inspector and the owner, but it does not replace the statutory inspection.

faq.q: Will heat or rain stop an ultrasonic examination?
faq.a: Heavy rain and lightning stop work for safety, and wet surfaces can disturb couplant. Hot surfaces are handled with high-temperature probes and couplant, but very hot metal may need scheduling around shutdowns or cooling.

faq.q: Does Atlantis act as API 510, 570 or 653 inspector?
faq.a: No. Under those codes the owner or its authorized inspector remains the inspector of record. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination and supplies the thickness data, weld findings and records the inspector relies on.

faq.q: How do I request ultrasonic testing in Tampa?
faq.a: Use the quote form and list the components, materials, wall thickness range, temperature, access method, governing code and any site orientation requirements. The request reaches a Level III reviewer and we reply within one business day.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Tampa, FL | MT
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection in Tampa, FL for weld cracks on port cranes, ship repair steel, structures and plant equipment, mobilized to site. Get a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Tampa, Florida
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out magnetic particle inspection (MPI, also called mag particle testing) in Tampa, Florida, looking for surface and near-surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel welds, castings and forgings. Typical work includes crane and rigging components, ship repair steel, structural connections and plant equipment around Tampa Bay. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. Send the part list through the MT inspection quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle testing is used in Tampa

Steel that is lifted, loaded, welded and repaired is where magnetic particle inspection earns its place, and Tampa has plenty of it. Port Tampa Bay is Florida's largest steel port, handles bulk materials such as cement, aggregates and phosphate, and hosts ship repair. That means mobile cranes, hoppers, grabs, conveyor frames, spreader hardware, mooring fittings and a steady flow of repair welds on hull framing, doublers and deck structures.

  • Lifting and handling equipment: crane hooks, shackles, padeyes, boom welds and slewing structures, where a fatigue crack grows from a stress riser in service.
  • Ship repair: repair welds on frames, brackets, rudder and shaft support structures, and the weld toes beside renewed plate.
  • Process plants: nozzle-to-shell welds, lug and support attachments on carbon steel vessels, and the welds on tank roof structures and walkways.
  • Bulk and cement handling: crusher frames, kiln support rollers' mounting structure, bucket elevator housings and wear-damaged weld repairs.
  • Fabrication shops and erection: weld toes on structural connections before painting, and repairs after gouging out a defect.

The salt-laden bay air adds a quiet problem. Coastal atmosphere attacks fillet weld toes and bolted joints, and a surface crack can hide under corrosion product until the coating is removed. Cleaning back to bare metal is part of the job, and MT is a good second look once the surface is exposed.

What magnetic particle testing finds and misses

MT magnetizes the part and applies fine iron particles. A crack that breaks the surface, or lies just under it, disturbs the magnetic field and holds the particles in a visible line. It is fast, shows the true shape of a crack, and needs little more than a yoke and clean steel.

The limits are strict. MT works only on ferromagnetic material, so carbon and low-alloy steels qualify, while austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and bronze do not respond. It finds surface and slightly subsurface flaws, not deep internal defects. Orientation matters, because a crack parallel to the field gives almost no indication, which is why a second examination at roughly right angles is required. Coatings thicker than the procedure allows, rough surfaces, and sharp changes in section can mask or mimic indications, and the technician has to tell a relevant crack from a nonrelevant magnetic writing at a geometry change.

Codes and acceptance criteria for MT in Tampa

Technique requirements come from ASME Section V Article 7, supported by ASTM E1444 for the practice and ASTM E709 as a guide. Acceptance depends on what the part is:

  • Pressure equipment: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 6 gives MT methods and acceptance for vessel welds.
  • Process piping: ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 describes magnetic particle examination, with criteria in Table 341.3.2.
  • Structural steel: AWS D1.1 sets visual and magnetic particle requirements for weld profiles and cracking, and AWS D1.5 governs steel bridges built for state DOT work.
  • In-service equipment: API 510, API 570 and API 653 call for NDE under the owner's inspection program, and the owner's authorized inspector stays responsible for the inspection.

Mechanical integrity under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) matters at the fuel and fertilizer plants that fall under process safety management, because inspection of crack-prone welds is part of showing that equipment is fit for continued service. For those plants Atlantis supplies the examination and the record. The mechanical integrity program and the fitness decision belong to the owner.

How magnetic particle examination is done

Most Tampa field work uses an electromagnetic yoke. Under Section V Article 7 an AC yoke must lift at least 10 pounds at the maximum pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke must lift at least 40 pounds; the lift is checked before use and at intervals. The yoke is placed across the weld in overlapping positions, then repeated with the poles turned about 90 degrees so cracks in either direction can show.

The particles come in two main forms. Dry powder in a contrasting color suits rough, warm surfaces and structural welds outdoors. Wet particles in a carrier, either visible or fluorescent, give higher sensitivity. Fluorescent particles are examined under UV-A light in a darkened area, which in the daylight and humidity of Tampa often means a portable tent or a shaded corner of a shop. Surfaces are cleaned of grease, scale and loose paint first, and a field indicator or a reference shim confirms the field direction and strength are adequate.

Where residual magnetism could interfere with later welding, machining or instrument operation, the part is demagnetized and checked with a gauss meter. Prods and coils are used for particular geometries, and the procedure states which applies to which component.

Who performs the work

MT is carried out by technicians qualified under Atlantis's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up the technique, examines and interprets; an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews reports. Procedures for Tampa MT work are approved by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis holds ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certification. Owners that need procedures written to their own code or customer specification can use Level III consulting, and the national magnetic particle testing page explains the general service.

Typical findings on lifting gear and repair welds

The cracks that magnetic particle inspection catches in a port or shipyard setting follow a few families. Fatigue cracks start at the root of a thread, at a sharp notch or at the toe of a fillet weld on a boom, and they grow a little with every load cycle until the part fails suddenly. Hydrogen-assisted cracking can appear in a high-strength or thick weld some time after it cools. Grinding cracks and arc strikes, small burns left by a careless electrode, create hard brittle spots that crack later. Repair welds placed on top of existing damage often crack along the fusion line, and those are the welds a careful owner wants examined before the equipment returns to service.

Not every indication is a defect. A line along a sharp corner, a change in section or the edge of a hardened zone can attract particles without being a crack. The technician reads the pattern, brushes or wipes the area, repeats the test and, where doubt remains, asks the Level III to review it before anything is accepted or cut out.

Surface condition, coatings and corrosion

Magnetic particle testing is more forgiving of surface condition than penetrant testing, but it still needs a clean, dry surface. Heavy rust, mill scale and thick paint reduce the strength of the field at the metal and hide small cracks, and so does a rough, undercut weld profile. Where a coating is left in place, the procedure sets the maximum thickness that was demonstrated to still show indications, and thicker coatings are removed locally. Wire brushing and light grinding are common; abrasive blasting is faster on large areas but may be restricted by the site.

After the test the particles are removed, bare metal is recoated or protected as the owner specifies, and any marks used to flag indications are cleaned up. Equipment that will go into marine or coastal service in Tampa should not be left bare, because new steel starts to rust within hours in humid air.

What the MT report contains

The report names the component, its tag or drawing number and its location, and the procedure and revision used. It lists the yoke or equipment model, the lift test or field strength check, the particle type and carrier, the lighting measurements for visible or fluorescent work, the surface condition and the technician and level. Each indication is recorded by location, orientation and length, with a sketch or photograph, and marked accepted or rejected against the code criterion cited. Repairs are re-examined and reported again after grinding or welding, so the file shows the original flaw, the repair and the final result.

Planning an MT job in Tampa

Magnetic particle work is sensitive to more than the steel. Wet methods tolerate a wide temperature range, but the part temperature has to stay within what the procedure is qualified for, and a steel surface in direct Florida summer sun can run far hotter than the air. Plan shaded or early-day work on exposed structures, or have the procedure qualified for the expected temperature. Humidity affects dry powder, which clumps and loses mobility, so wet technique is often chosen in the wet season.

Afternoon storms, lightning and wind interrupt rigging and crane inspections at the port, and hurricane season brings pre-storm tie-down and post-storm damage checks that compete for the same crews. Port and plant sites usually require orientation and identification before entry, and hot work or confined space rules add time. Atlantis has no office in Tampa, so technicians are mobilized from outside the area and travel is included in the quote.

MT, PT or UT for your Tampa job

Pick the method by material and question. MT suits carbon steel with a surface crack concern and is quicker than penetrant on welds. If the steel is stainless, aluminum or any nonmagnetic alloy, use liquid penetrant testing in Tampa. If wall loss or an internal weld flaw is the concern, use ultrasonic testing in Tampa. A common pairing at fuel terminals is UT thickness on the shell and MT on the welds around a repair patch. For the state context see inspection services in Florida, and for method theory the magnetic particle testing complete guide and the MT versus PT comparison.

Training your own MT technicians

Companies in Tampa that run their own maintenance can train inspectors rather than outsource. Atlantis offers MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 courses, the magnetic particle testing training overview, and NDT training in Tampa. Your company's own written practice completes the certification, because under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies. The SNT-TC-1A eligibility checker helps a candidate see the hours needed.

faq.q: What is the difference between MPI and magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: They are the same method. Magnetic particle inspection, MPI, mag particle testing and MT all describe magnetizing a ferromagnetic part and using iron particles to reveal surface and near-surface cracks.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle inspection be done on stainless steel piping in Tampa?
faq.a: Not on austenitic stainless steel, because it is not ferromagnetic and will not hold the field. Use liquid penetrant testing for stainless piping, which works on any clean non-porous surface where a flaw is open to the surface.

faq.q: How thick a coating can stay on the part during MT?
faq.a: The procedure sets a maximum coating thickness that was demonstrated to still show indications, and thicker coatings are removed locally. Corroded or flaking paint should always be cleaned off before the weld is examined.

faq.q: Why is the weld examined twice with the yoke?
faq.a: A crack parallel to the magnetic field gives almost no indication. Section V Article 7 therefore requires two examinations with the field at roughly right angles so that cracks in any direction are detected.

faq.q: Does hot Florida weather affect magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: Yes. Part temperature has to stay inside the range the procedure was qualified for, and sunlit steel can exceed air temperature. Dry powder also clumps in humidity, so wet particles or shaded scheduling are often used.

faq.q: Does Atlantis demagnetize parts after MT?
faq.a: Where residual magnetism could interfere with later welding, machining or instruments, the part is demagnetized and checked with a gauss meter. The requirement is stated in the job scope and recorded in the report.

faq.q: Which codes apply to MT on welds at a Tampa terminal or plant?
faq.a: Technique follows ASME Section V Article 7. Acceptance comes from the construction or in-service code, such as ASME Section VIII Appendix 6 for vessels, B31.3 for process piping, or AWS D1.1 for structural steel.

faq.q: How do I get a quote for magnetic particle inspection in Tampa?
faq.a: Use the quote form and list the parts, material, coating condition, location, access, governing code and any site orientation requirement. Atlantis has no office in Tampa, so technicians travel to your site and we reply within one business day.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing & Dye Penetrant (PT) | Tampa, FL
pt.description: Dye penetrant inspection in Tampa, FL for stainless piping, aluminum, weld repairs and machinery, plus ship and plant work. Mobilized to site. Get a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Tampa, Florida
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing, often called dye penetrant inspection or PT, in Tampa, Florida. It reveals cracks, laps and porosity that are open to the surface of stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and carbon steel alike. Typical Tampa work covers stainless process piping, weld repairs, ship repair fittings and machinery castings. Technicians are mobilized to your site. Send the part list with the PT inspection quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where dye penetrant testing is used in Tampa

PT is the method owners reach for when the metal will not take a magnetic field. Tampa has a lot of that metal. Fertilizer and chemical processing uses stainless piping and fittings because of acid service. Food and beverage plants, including juice and citrus processing near the bay, use stainless tanks and sanitary piping. Ship repair at the port deals in aluminum, bronze and stainless fittings alongside steel. Cement and aggregate operations have cast and machined parts that crack in service.

  • Stainless process piping: root and cap passes on fertilizer and chemical lines, where a crack that opens to the surface can leak a hazardous fluid.
  • Sanitary and food-grade vessels: weld seams on stainless tanks in beverage and food production.
  • Marine components: propeller and shaft fittings, valve bodies, aluminum structure and repair welds on yard work.
  • Rotating and heavy equipment: pump casings, gearbox housings, and cast parts that show fatigue cracking.
  • Weld preparation and repair: checking a gouged-out groove before rewelding and a final surface examination after grinding.

What penetrant testing finds and misses

A low-viscosity liquid is applied to a clean surface, enters any surface-breaking discontinuity by capillary action, and after the excess is removed a developer draws it back out as a visible indication. Cracks, laps, seams, cold shuts and pinholes show well. PT works on any non-porous material, magnetic or not.

It will only find flaws that are open to the surface. A crack closed by smeared metal, a hairline sealed under paint or an indication filled with dirt, grease or blasting media gives nothing. Rough or porous surfaces hold penetrant and cause background that hides small indications. Shot blasting and heavy grinding can peen the surface shut, so etching or careful preparation is sometimes needed before the test. The method says nothing about wall thickness or subsurface flaws.

Codes and acceptance criteria for PT in Tampa

The technique is written to ASME Section V Article 6, with ASTM E165 as the general-industry practice. Acceptance depends on the part:

  • Pressure vessels: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 8, covering liquid penetrant methods and acceptance for welds and surfaces.
  • Process piping: ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 and the criteria in Table 341.3.2.
  • Power piping: ASME B31.1 for steam and feedwater systems.
  • Structure and bridges: AWS D1.1 for buildings, AWS D1.5 for bridges, and AWS D1.6 for stainless structural welds.
  • In-service equipment: API 510 and API 570 programs rely on the owner's authorized inspector, with Atlantis supplying the examination and records.

Section V Article 6 also controls the penetrant materials. Where the product contacts austenitic stainless steel or nickel alloys, the contaminant content of penetrants and cleaners, such as halogens and sulfur, has to be limited and documented, because those elements can damage the metal. That matters in Tampa, where stainless equipment sits in a coastal atmosphere.

How penetrant examination is done

Surface preparation comes first and decides the outcome. Oil, grease, scale, paint, rust and weld spatter are removed, and the part is dry before penetrant is applied. Then comes the penetrant itself. A visible red dye is the usual choice for field work in daylight, and a fluorescent type is used when higher sensitivity is wanted and the area can be darkened for UV-A light. The penetrant dwells on the surface for the time stated in the procedure.

Excess penetrant is removed in a controlled way. A solvent-removable system, with wipe and a slightly dampened cloth, is typical on site. Water-washable and post-emulsified systems are used in shop settings. The developer, most often a thin layer of nonaqueous suspension, is applied evenly and allowed time to draw out any trapped liquid. The technician examines the surface at the specified times and records what shows. The procedure also sets the light level on the surface for visible work.

Because indications can be false when the surface is contaminated or the developer is too thick, the examination is repeated if doubt remains: the part is recleaned and retested rather than guessed at.

Penetrant types, methods and sensitivity

ASTM E165 and Section V Article 6 sort penetrant materials by type and method. Type I penetrants are fluorescent and are examined under UV-A light; Type II penetrants are visible dyes that show in white light. The method describes how excess penetrant is removed: water-washable, post-emulsified with a lipophilic or hydrophilic emulsifier, or solvent-removable. Sensitivity levels run from low to ultra-high for fluorescent materials, and a higher level finds finer cracks but also shows more background on rough surfaces.

Field work on a Tampa tank, vessel or pipe usually uses a visible, solvent-removable system because it needs no water supply, no darkened booth and no power, and the materials come in aerosol cans that are easy to carry. A shop-based inspection of machined or cast parts can use fluorescent water-washable materials for higher sensitivity. The procedure names the system, and a system is not interchanged with another mid-job. Penetrant materials that were used with one system are not reused with a different one, because residue from one family can ruin the sensitivity of another.

Reading indications and common flaws

After development the technician separates relevant indications from nonrelevant ones. A relevant indication is caused by a discontinuity; a nonrelevant one comes from a scratch, a rough surface or penetrant trapped in a thread or a crevice. Under the acceptance sections of the codes a linear indication is one with a length of more than three times its width, and a rounded indication is anything else. Linear indications generally indicate cracks, laps and seams and are judged much more strictly than rounded ones.

On equipment around Tampa Bay the flaws of most interest are fatigue cracks in castings and shafts, cracks at weld toes and in repair welds, and stress corrosion cracking in austenitic stainless steel, which can start in warm, humid, chloride-rich atmospheres on the outside of piping and tanks. Surface-breaking stress corrosion cracks branch and can be missed by eye, so penetrant testing is often the method that reveals them. Only the indications that exceed the acceptance criteria are rejected, and the report records the borderline ones too.

Who performs the work

PT technicians are qualified under Atlantis's written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians apply the materials, interpret and report. Procedures are approved, and reports reviewed, by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT and the reports are reviewed by him. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. The national penetrant testing page describes the service in general. For custom procedures see Level III consulting.

What the PT report contains

The report identifies the part, its location and tag, the procedure and revision, and the penetrant family, type, method and developer with their manufacturer and batch information. It records the cleaner used, the surface preparation, the part temperature, the dwell and development times, the lighting used and the technician and level. Indications are recorded with location, size and type (linear or rounded) against the acceptance criteria named, with a photograph or sketch. A rejected indication is traced through repair and retest so the final record closes the loop.

Planning a PT job in Tampa

The standard temperature range in Section V Article 6 for the part and the penetrant materials is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Tampa winter nights are mild enough to stay inside that range, but a steel or stainless surface in summer sun can easily exceed 125 degrees, and outside the range the procedure has to be qualified at the actual temperature. Plan work on exposed tanks and piping for shade or cooler hours, or arrange the qualification beforehand.

Humidity and dew matter too, because moisture on a surface contaminates the test and dilutes the penetrant. Afternoon storms and wind can wash off or contaminate a prepared surface, and the area may need shelter. Fuel and fertilizer sites add access rules, hot work and gas testing controls that affect the sequence of preparation and cleanup. Penetrant waste and solvent wipes have to be handled under the site's rules. Atlantis has no office in Tampa; technicians are mobilized to your site and the quote includes travel.

Safety, waste and site rules for penetrant work

Penetrant systems are chemicals, and Tampa's fuel and fertilizer sites treat them accordingly. Aerosol cleaners and developers are flammable and release vapors, so hot work permits and gas testing may affect when and where the examination can start, and enclosed spaces need ventilation and entry controls. Safety data sheets for each product are reviewed with the site's safety staff before work begins.

Used wipes, empty cans and rinse water are waste, and the site's rules decide where they go. The examination is planned with that in mind: how much solvent will be used, where wipes are collected, and who takes them away. Where the part is going into oxygen, chlorine or other reactive service, the final cleaning step and the cleanliness inspection are specified in the scope, because residual penetrant is a contaminant in those systems.

PT, MT or UT for your Tampa job

PT is usually the answer for nonmagnetic metals and for surface-breaking flaws on any clean part. For carbon steel welds with a crack concern, magnetic particle inspection in Tampa is quicker and also finds slightly subsurface flaws. For wall loss or an internal weld flaw, use ultrasonic testing in Tampa. See inspection services in Florida for the wider scope and the ASME Section V Article 6 explainer for the requirements behind the method.

Training your own PT technicians

PT is among the quickest methods to learn, which makes it suitable for in-house teams in plants and yards. Atlantis offers PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 courses, a penetrant testing simulator for practice and the Tampa training page. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer completes certification under its own written practice.

faq.q: Are dye penetrant inspection and liquid penetrant testing different methods?
faq.a: No, the names are interchangeable. Dye penetrant inspection, liquid penetrant testing, penetrant testing and PT all describe applying a liquid that enters surface-breaking flaws and is drawn out again by a developer.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing be used on stainless steel and aluminum in Tampa?
faq.a: Yes. PT works on any clean non-porous material, including stainless steel, aluminum and nickel alloys, which magnetic particle testing cannot examine. For stainless the penetrant materials must meet contaminant limits.

faq.q: What temperature range applies to penetrant testing?
faq.a: The standard range in ASME Section V Article 6 is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and materials. Outside it the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature, which matters for summer sun on steel.

faq.q: Why does surface preparation matter so much for PT?
faq.a: Penetrant cannot enter a flaw that is plugged with paint, scale, oil, blasting media or smeared metal. Poor cleaning hides cracks, so preparation is usually the step that decides whether the examination is valid.

faq.q: Does PT find internal weld flaws or wall loss?
faq.a: No. Penetrant testing finds only flaws open to the surface. Wall loss and internal weld flaws need ultrasonic testing, and surface cracks in carbon steel can also be examined with magnetic particle inspection.

faq.q: Which acceptance criteria apply to PT on Tampa piping and vessels?
faq.a: Technique follows ASME Section V Article 6, and acceptance comes from the governing code, such as ASME Section VIII Appendix 8 for vessels or B31.3 Table 341.3.2 for process piping.

faq.q: Does Atlantis supply the penetrant materials documentation for stainless work?
faq.a: Yes. The report lists penetrant, remover and developer by manufacturer and batch and records the contaminant data supplied with them, so the owner can show the materials were suitable for stainless steel or nickel alloys.

faq.q: How do I ask for liquid penetrant testing in Tampa?
faq.a: Use the quote form and describe the parts, material, surface condition, temperature, location, access, governing code and site orientation needs. Atlantis has no office in Tampa, technicians travel to your site, and we reply within one business day.

rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) in Tampa, Florida: What Atlantis Offers
rt.html:
Atlantis does not perform industrial radiography anywhere in the United States. Industrial radiography is a licensed activity, regulated by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission under 10 CFR Part 34 or by the equivalent rules of an Agreement State, and it is not a service Atlantis offers in Tampa or anywhere else in the country. If you searched for radiography in Tampa, this page explains what we can do instead and when each option fits.

Ultrasonic testing as the volumetric alternative in Tampa

For many welds, ultrasonic examination looks through the volume of the joint much as radiography does, and it needs no radiation barrier, no exclusion zone and no interruption of neighboring work. That matters on a busy Tampa terminal or in a plant where adjacent crews cannot be cleared. The ultrasonic testing service in Tampa includes shear-wave weld examination by Level II technicians mobilized to your site.

Substituting UT for RT is a code decision, not a preference. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 has its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and ASME Section VIII permits UT in place of RT only under specific conditions. The substitution has to be agreed with the owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector before the job starts. UT is also not a one-for-one copy: it responds best to planar flaws such as lack of fusion and cracks, while radiography records volumetric flaws such as porosity differently.

ASNT Level III radiography services that need no radiation license

Reviewing radiographs does not involve a source, so it needs no radiation license. An ASNT Level III, the founder Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, can assist in these ways:

  • Independent review of radiographs, film or digital images, and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code.
  • A second read on disputed or borderline indications before a weld is cut out or accepted.
  • Review of an RT contractor's procedure and written practice against the contract and the code.

This is review work performed from records and images; it is not a substitute for the shoot itself. Owners who need radiography performed must hire a licensed radiographer. For help writing or auditing procedures see Level III consulting and written practice development.

Radiography theory training

If your goal is to understand radiography, the theory side can be learned without a source. The radiographic testing Level 2 course is available as theory training for people who will later work under a licensed employer. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its personnel, and radiation safety training and licensing are separate requirements set by the regulator. See NDT training in Tampa for the wider training options.

Other surface and thickness methods in Tampa

Atlantis also performs magnetic particle inspection and liquid penetrant testing in Tampa for surface cracks, and the Florida inspection hub lists the state coverage. Technicians travel to your site, because Atlantis has no office in Tampa. To discuss a UT alternative, a radiograph review or training, use the quote form and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Is radiographic testing available from Atlantis in Tampa?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, because industrial radiography is a licensed activity under NRC rules or Agreement State equivalents. It offers UT, radiograph review and RT theory training instead.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my Tampa welds?
faq.a: That depends on the construction code and on what the owner agrees. B31.3, API 1104, AWS D1.1 and Section VIII each treat UT differently, so settle the substitution with the owner, engineer and authorized inspector first.

faq.q: Can an ASNT Level III review radiographs without a radiation license?
faq.a: Yes. Reviewing film or digital images and technique sheets involves no radioactive source or X-ray equipment, so no radiation license is needed. The review compares the records with ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code.

faq.q: Does Atlantis recommend a radiography contractor in Tampa?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not name or recommend radiography contractors. Choose a licensed radiographer yourself, and Atlantis can review the contractor procedure, written practice and resulting radiographs if you ask for that service.

faq.q: Is radiography training available through Atlantis?
faq.a: Theory training is available through the radiographic testing Level 2 course. Radiation safety training and licensing are set by the regulator, and under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its personnel after the required hours.
